summaries.example: Imagine a blue ball. Dharmakīrti would say the particular ball is real because it can do something, such as bounce or make a mark. But “blueness” by itself is not an extra object hiding beside the ball. It is a way people group similar things in thought and speech.
summaries.summary: Dharmakīrti was an Indian Buddhist philosopher known for careful thinking about reality, change, causes, knowledge, and language. His school was nominalist: it treated individual things as fully real, while general kinds were useful ideas rather than separate objects. A thing is real when it has causal power, meaning that it can produce effects. Since a real thing is always doing something, Dharmakīrti argued that it cannot remain exactly the same forever. It exists for a moment and then becomes a new moment. He also explained how we know things. Perception gives us direct awareness of particular things, while inference uses reasons to reach conclusions. Language is useful even though words often stand for general ideas that are not found as separate objects in reality. Dharmakīrti tried to explain this by connecting things, perceptions, thoughts, and words through causes. His work also applied reasoning to Buddhist teachings, although this overview mainly emphasizes his metaphysics.
key_ideas: Dharmakīrti says individual things are real because they can produce effects.
General kinds, such as “redness,” help people think and talk, but they are not separate things in the world.
Everything real is momentary: it changes into a new thing moment by moment.
He explains causes through the powers things have and through careful observations of what happens together.
He distinguishes perception from inference: seeing a particular thing differs from thinking about a general idea.
summaries.why_it_matters: Dharmakīrti shows how difficult questions can be explored with clear tests and arguments. His ideas ask us to look closely at what counts as real, how change works, and how words connect with the world. They also show that a philosopher may use logic both to study everyday knowledge and to discuss religious beliefs.

important_terms.definition: A real, individual thing, such as one blue ball. Dharmakīrti says particulars can have effects and are real in the strongest sense.
A general idea, such as “blueness” or “ballness,” that helps us group things. Dharmakīrti says universals are useful but not independently real.
The ability of something to make a difference or produce an effect. Dharmakīrti uses this as a test for what is truly real.
The view that things are made up of individual cases rather than real shared kinds.
The idea that every real thing lasts for only one moment and is replaced by a new moment.
A way of finding out that uses direct experience rather than a chain of ideas.
A way of finding out by using a reason, such as noticing smoke and thinking there is fire.

questions_to_think_about: Is a general idea like “tree” a real thing, or is it a useful way to group many trees?
Does something have to make a difference before we call it real?
If a thing changes every moment, why does it seem to stay the same?
How could you test whether one event really causes another?

summaries.example: Suppose smoke is seen rising from a hill. A Dharmakīrtian analysis asks more than whether smoke and fire often appear together. It asks whether smoke’s being smoke is tied to having been produced by fire, and whether fire has the causal capacity to produce smoke under suitable conditions. Observation of co-presence and co-absence helps us establish the connection, but the connection is not treated as a mere accidental pattern.
summaries.summary: Dharmakīrti develops a Buddhist metaphysics in which only particulars are ultimately real. His nominalism rejects real universals such as blueness or cowhood; such generalities are conceptual fictions useful for thought and communication. The decisive mark of reality is causal efficacy: a real entity must be able to produce an effect. This criterion also supports momentariness. If a thing were permanent and wholly unchanged, it could not explain a succession of different effects; if surrounding conditions alone changed, those conditions would appear to be the true causes. Dharmakīrti presents two arguments for momentariness, but the argument from existence and causal activity is treated as more promising than the older argument that things perish spontaneously. His causal theory of properties identifies what a thing is with its powers or fitness to produce results in complete circumstances, rather than separating a substance from properties that it owns. His account of causality combines empirical methods—examining co-presence and co-absence—with a stronger idea of a connection grounded in the causal natures of things. This creates an interpretive tension often compared with the contrast between regularity theories of causation and theories that locate causal necessity in the relata. The same causal emphasis appears in his account of language. Perception is non-conceptual awareness of particulars; inference is conceptual and operates with general representations. Through apoha and causal chains linking particulars to perceptions, thoughts, and utterances, Dharmakīrti explains how words can refer without requiring real universals. The broader entry also connects these positions to Buddhist epistemology, logic, religious reasoning, and debates with non-Buddhist schools.
key_ideas: Dharmakīrti’s metaphysics combines nominalism with a criterion of causal efficacy: what can perform causal work is real, while universals and other pseudo-entities lack such powers.
Reality is particular and momentary. Enduring objects are series of qualitatively similar moments, not numerically identical substances persisting through time.

His stronger argument for momentariness begins from existence and causal activity: an unchanging thing could not produce different effects in sequence, since changing circumstances would do the causal work.
Properties are understood causally rather than as separate universals inhering in bare substances. A thing’s properties consist in its powers or fitness to produce effects in suitable circumstances.

Dharmakīrti distinguishes how causality is discovered from what causality is. We investigate co-presence and co-absence empirically, yet he also appeals to a connection grounded in the natures of causes and effects.
Perception concerns particulars, whereas inference concerns conceptual generalities. Apoha helps explain how language can be about the world even though general kinds are not independently real.
summaries.why_it_matters: Dharmakīrti’s philosophy brings metaphysics, epistemology, philosophy of language, and logic into one system. It asks whether reality is fundamentally made of enduring kinds or changing particulars, whether causation is more than regular succession, and how thought can represent a world that does not contain the same categories found in language. These problems remain recognizable in contemporary debates about universals, causation, reference, justification, and idealism.

important_terms.definition: The view that only individual, causally effective entities are ultimately real; general kinds are conceptual constructions used in thought and language.
An individual entity, or particular, that exists at one place and time and has causal efficacy.
A general kind or feature, such as blueness, treated by Dharmakīrti as customarily accepted rather than ultimately real.
The capacity to produce effects. For Dharmakīrti, causal efficacy is central to the distinction between reality and conceptual fiction.
The thesis that every real entity exists only for a moment and is replaced by a numerically different entity.
A source of knowledge that presents particulars without conceptual or linguistic construction.
A conceptual source of knowledge that reaches a conclusion through a reliable reason.
Dharmakīrti’s account of concepts and reference through exclusions of what is other, supplemented by causal links between things, perceptions, thoughts, and words.

questions_to_think_about: Does causal efficacy provide a satisfactory boundary between reality and useful fiction?
Does the argument from causal activity successfully rule out permanent entities, or could an unchanging cause act through changing circumstances?
Can a causal theory of reference explain shared words without smuggling in real universals?
How should we interpret Dharmakīrti’s claim that causal connections are stronger than observed regularities while still being discovered through fallible experience?
What changes when the school’s account is interpreted through external realism rather than Yogācāra idealism?

summaries.example: A class notices that a certain plant can help reduce fever. The plants do not all look exactly alike, so Dharmakīrti need not say they share one hidden “fever-curing” universal. Instead, each plant is an individual with its own particular causal ability. They can be grouped because their different abilities lead to a similar result, not because one extra common object exists inside them.
summaries.summary: Dharmakīrti was an important Indian Buddhist philosopher whose work examined what exists, how change happens, and how people gain knowledge. His school takes a nominalist position. It says that individual particulars are real, while universals—general kinds such as “blueness” or “animal”—are not extra things existing alongside their examples. They are useful ways of organizing thought and language. The key difference between reality and fiction is causal power. A particular is real because it can produce an effect. This idea leads to Dharmakīrti’s theory of momentariness. Everything real exists for only one moment and is replaced by a new moment. He considers an older argument that things naturally perish as soon as they arise, but the source presents that argument as unclear. His own more promising argument says that something that produces different effects must change. A permanent, unchanged thing could not be the real cause of a changing series of results; if only outside conditions changed, those new conditions would seem to do the causal work. Dharmakīrti also explains properties in causal terms. A thing’s feature is connected to what it can do in a complete set of conditions, rather than being a separate universal stored inside it. This approach creates an interesting problem about causation. We discover causes by observing what is present when an effect occurs and absent when it does not, but Dharmakīrti also treats causal connections as grounded in the natures or powers of things, not merely in repeated patterns. key_ideas: Dharmakīrti’s school says that particulars are fully real, but universals are convenient constructions for thinking and speaking.
Causal power is the test of reality: real things can bring about changes or results.
Because real things are causally active, Dharmakīrti argues that they cannot stay exactly the same across time.
He gives a stronger and a weaker argument for momentariness; the argument from existence and causal activity is presented as the more convincing one.
Properties are not separate objects attached to things. They are understood through what each particular can do in the right conditions.
Perception gives access to particulars, while inference uses concepts and reasons. Apoha helps explain how language can still talk about the world.
summaries.why_it_matters: Dharmakīrti matters because he connects questions that are often studied separately. His ideas about momentary things affect his account of causation; his account of causation helps explain properties; and his theory of concepts helps explain language and reasoning. Studying him also shows that Buddhist philosophy included detailed debates about reality, evidence, logic, and the limits of certainty.

important_terms.definition: The view that individual things are real, while general kinds are ideas people use to organize experience rather than separate objects.
One individual thing, such as one plant or one sound, rather than a kind shared by many things.
A general feature or kind, such as redness or plant-kind, which Dharmakīrti treats as conceptually useful but not ultimately real.
The power of a thing to produce an effect. Dharmakīrti treats this as a major sign that something is real.
The claim that real things exist only moment by moment, with a new thing arising at each moment.
Knowledge gained directly, without first reasoning from a general idea.
Knowledge reached by using a reason, such as concluding that there is fire because smoke is present.
A Buddhist theory explaining concepts as exclusions of what does not belong, with Dharmakīrti adding an important causal explanation of how words connect to things.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a philosopher reject the idea that many red things share one real universal called redness?
If an object changes every moment, why do people normally call it the same object?
Would an unchanging thing be able to cause different effects at different times?
Are repeated observations enough to prove a cause, or do we need something deeper?
How might words be connected to real things if general categories are not real objects?
